title: Factor and Cluster Analysis
breadcrumb: Module 8 · Multivariate Analysis · Factor and cluster analysis
objectives: Explain the common-factor model and distinguish common variance from uniqueness.
Explain factor rotation and recognise varimax.
Distinguish factor analysis from principal component analysis.
Describe hierarchical and k-means clustering and common linkage rules.

howto: For factor analysis, specify the common-factor model, inspect loadings, calculate communalities and uniquenesses, then interpret a rotated solution. For clustering, define the cases and variables, standardise when appropriate, choose a distance and linkage or k, and interpret groups with substantive caution.

scenes.title: Two different multivariate questions
body: Multivariate analysis asks whether observed variables share a smaller number of underlying dimensions, or whether cases can be divided into groups with similar profiles.
Factor analysis explains correlations among variables through latent common factors.
Cluster analysis groups observations or objects using similarity or distance.

items.ask: Factor analysis primarily seeks to group what?
refresh: The diagonal entries of a covariance matrix are the variances of the individual observed variables. Each value quantifies the spread of one coordinate around its population mean and determines the scale of that variable in the multivariate data cloud.

Off-diagonal entries are covariances. They record how two variables vary together; positive covariance indicates that above-average values tend to occur together, while negative covariance indicates opposite movement. These entries determine the orientation of the data cloud.

The inverse covariance matrix reverses the scale information and accounts for dependence among coordinates. In Mahalanobis geometry, directions with large natural variance receive less weight, while unusual directions receive more weight.

ask.q: To discover hidden dimensions behind ten questionnaire items, which method is relevant?
ask.nudge: The goal is to explain correlations among variables.

scenes.title: Latent traits behind observed variables
scenes.objective: Understand the motivation for factor analysis.
body: Vocabulary, reading comprehension, grammar and verbal reasoning scores may correlate because they share a broader latent ability.
Factor analysis represents this shared pattern using fewer common factors. The factors are not directly observed; they are inferred from a covariance or correlation matrix.
A useful solution must be statistically defensible and substantively interpretable. The algorithm does not name the latent construct.

scenario.title: A student skills survey
body: A university measures ten indicators of academic engagement: reading frequency, library use, assignment planning, class participation and peer discussion. Many indicators are positively correlated. The researcher suspects that a few broader dimensions may explain the shared pattern.

Exploratory factor analysis investigates whether correlations are organised around fewer latent factors. The researcher examines loadings and names factors only after considering what the variables measure.
scenario.q: What is the main reason to use factor analysis?
scenario.answer: To explain shared correlations among observed indicators using fewer latent factors.

ask.q: Are latent factors directly measured in the original questionnaire?
ask.nudge: They are inferred from observed variables.

blocks.body: X=μ+ΛF+ε. X is the p-vector of observed variables, F the q-vector of common factors, Λ the loading matrix, and ε the variable-specific components.
If Cov(F)=I, Cov(ε)=Ψ and common factors are uncorrelated with unique components, then Σ=ΛΛ′+Ψ, with Ψ diagonal.
For variable i, hᵢ²=Σⱼ λᵢⱼ² in the usual orthogonal solution. For a standardised variable, ψᵢ=1−hᵢ².
A larger absolute loading indicates a stronger association between the observed variable and that factor. The sign indicates direction.

ask.q: In the orthogonal common-factor model, what does Ψ represent?
ask.nudge: It is the diagonal covariance matrix of variable-specific components.

scenes.title: Calculate communalities
scenes.problem: A standardised variable has loadings 0.6 and 0.5 on two retained orthogonal factors. Find its communality and uniqueness.

steps.why: The contribution of a factor to communality is its squared loading.
Add squared loadings across retained orthogonal factors.
The two factors explain 61% of the variable's variance in this standardised model.
The remaining 39% is specific plus error variance.

ask.q: If a third orthogonal factor with loading 0.3 is retained, what is the new communality?
ask.nudge: Add 0.3 squared to the current communality.

scenes.intro: Try to answer before revealing each definition.

items.a: The variance of an observed variable explained by retained common factors.
The variable-specific plus error variance not explained by common factors.
An unobserved common dimension inferred from observed variables.

scenes.title: Extraction, rotation and PCA distinction
scenes.objective: Recognise rotation and separate PCA from factor analysis.

blocks.body: An extraction method estimates a lower-dimensional common-factor representation from the covariance or correlation structure. The number of factors is informed by theory and diagnostics.
Rotation changes factor-axis orientation to produce a more interpretable loading pattern. Varimax is orthogonal; oblique rotations permit correlated factors.
PCA constructs linear combinations to explain total observed variance. Common factor analysis models shared covariance and separates common variance from uniqueness.
Scree plots, eigenvalue rules, parallel analysis and substantive interpretability can inform the choice. No single mechanical rule replaces judgement.

ask.q: Which rotation keeps the rotated factors orthogonal?
ask.nudge: It is the widely used variance-maximising orthogonal rotation.

scenes.title: Interpret a rotated loading pattern
scenes.objective: Read a simple factor loading matrix.
scenes.problem: A rotated solution has two factors. A loads (0.82, 0.10), B loads (0.76, 0.18), and C loads (0.08, 0.79). Give a simple interpretation.
hints: Compare absolute loadings within each row.
A and B load mainly on the first factor; C loads mainly on the second.
Name factors only after considering what the variables measure.
scenes.answer: A and B define the first factor; C defines the second. Substantive labels require variable descriptions.
scenes.check: A and B → Factor 1; C → Factor 2.

solution.why: Both variables are strongly associated with the first factor.
Variable C is primarily associated with the second factor.

solution.math: Use item meanings to name factors.
solution.why: Loadings show statistical association; interpretation needs subject-matter context.

ask.q: Why is it risky to name Factor 1 without knowing what A and B measure?
ask.nudge: A numerical pattern alone does not reveal the substantive construct.

scenes.title: Hierarchical cluster analysis

blocks.body: Start with each observation as its own cluster. Repeatedly merge the two closest clusters until one cluster remains or the desired number is reached.
Cluster distance is the minimum distance between any cross-cluster pair. It can produce chaining.
Complete linkage uses the maximum cross-cluster pairwise distance. Average linkage uses the average of those distances.
Ward's method merges the pair causing the smallest increase in within-cluster sum of squares. A dendrogram displays the sequence and height of merges.

ask.q: Which linkage is most associated with chaining?
ask.nudge: It merges clusters whenever at least one cross-cluster pair is close.

hints: Write all four distances between points in different clusters.
Single linkage takes the minimum; complete linkage takes the maximum.
scenes.answer: Single linkage is 2 and complete linkage is 9.

scenario.title: Grouping retail outlets
body: A retail chain compares outlets using two standardised measures: monthly customer growth and average basket value. Each outlet is represented by a point in a two-dimensional feature space. The analyst first forms small groups of nearby outlets and then considers whether to merge two existing groups. The distance between groups depends on the linkage definition, not merely on the distance between their centroids.

If the analyst uses single linkage, one close pair of outlets can connect two otherwise widely separated groups. Complete linkage instead considers the farthest cross-group pair and tends to favour more compact clusters. Average linkage uses the mean of all cross-group pair distances. The analyst should explain which rule was used before interpreting the resulting dendrogram, because different linkage choices can produce different group structures.
scenario.q: Which linkage rule uses the largest cross-cluster pairwise distance?

scenes.title: Read the linkage rule
scenes.problem: Cluster A contains points 1 and 8; cluster B contains points 4 and 10 on a one-dimensional scale. Find single-linkage and complete-linkage distances.

steps.why: Only pairs with one point from each cluster are considered.

steps.say: Take the minimum for single linkage.
steps.why: Single linkage uses the nearest cross-cluster pair.

steps.say: Take the maximum for complete linkage.
steps.why: Complete linkage uses the farthest cross-cluster pair.

ask.nudge: It aggregates all four cross-cluster distances.

scenes.title: k-means clustering
scenes.objective: Describe the k-means algorithm and limitations.

blocks.body: For chosen k, k-means minimises ΣⱼΣᵢ∈Cⱼ ||xᵢ−cⱼ||², where cⱼ is the centroid of cluster j.
Choose k initial centres; assign each observation to its nearest centre; recompute each centre as the mean of its assigned observations; repeat until stable.
Results depend on initial centres. The method is sensitive to outliers and variable scale, and favours roughly compact, centroid-based groups.
An elbow plot compares within-cluster sum of squares across k. Silhouette width assesses cohesion and separation. These diagnostics support, but do not mechanically settle, the choice.

ask.q: Why standardise variables measured in rupees and years before k-means?
ask.nudge: Euclidean distance is affected by the scale of each coordinate.

scenes.title: Factor or cluster? Avoid the traps
scenes.intro: Decide whether each statement is correct.

items.claim: Factor analysis explains covariance among variables using latent factors.
items.why: Its target is the shared structure among observed variables.

items.claim: Cluster analysis primarily groups variables into latent dimensions.
items.why: Basic cluster analysis groups observations or objects, not latent dimensions among variables.

items.claim: k-means automatically determines the number of clusters k.
items.why: The user specifies k before running standard k-means.

ask.q: Which method segments customers into groups based on their profiles?
ask.nudge: The objects to be grouped are the customers.

scenes.title: Exam-ready method selector
body: Factor analysis explains shared covariance among observed variables through latent common factors. Loadings describe variable–factor relationships; communalities and uniquenesses partition variance.
Rotation improves interpretability. Varimax is orthogonal, while oblique rotations allow correlated factors. PCA explains total variance; common factor analysis models shared variance.

Hierarchical clustering builds nested groups using linkage rules and displays them in a dendrogram. Single uses minimum distance, complete maximum, average the mean, and Ward minimises the increase in within-cluster sum of squares.
k-means partitions observations into a chosen k clusters by minimising within-cluster squared distances. Standardisation, initialisation, outliers and interpretation matter.

ask.q: What is the quickest distinction between factor analysis and cluster analysis?
ask.nudge: One groups variables through latent dimensions; the other groups cases.
